title: God's action is the creature's own action as receiving its being from God, not a distinct action on the will
source_text: XXVIII. Deinde consequenter docent actionem causae primae concurrentis cum causa secunda, non esse actionem reipsa diversam ab actione causae secundae, sed illam ipsam actionem, quatenus esse suum a causa prima accipit. Ita quum Deus, verbi causa, cum voluntate concurrit in volendi, vel nolendi actu, ipse non exerit, ex eorum mente, actionem aliquam in voluntatem, distinctam ab actione voluntatis ipsius; sed tantum esse confert actioni voluntatis simul cum voluntate, & actionem illam conservat. Ac proinde divina hac in parte cooperatio non est aliquid diversum a volitione nostra, sed ipsa nostra volitio, quatenus a Deo immediate pendet quoad sui productionem & conservationem.
pass_a_gloss: Next consequently they teach that the action of the first cause concurring with the second cause, is not an action really different from the action of the second cause, but that very action, in so far as it receives its being from the first cause. So when God, for example, concurs with the will in the act of willing, or of refusing, he does not put forth, according to their mind, any action on the will, distinct from the action of the will itself; but only confers being on the action of the will together with the will, and preserves that action. And accordingly the divine cooperation in this part is not something different from our volition, but our volition itself, in so far as it depends immediately on God as to its production and preservation.
pass_b_english: Next, and consistently with this, they teach that the action of the first cause concurring with the secondary cause is not an action really distinct from that of the secondary cause. It is that same action, considered as receiving its being from the first cause.

So when God concurs with the will in an act of willing or refusing, he does not, on their view, exert on the will an action distinct from the will's own. He only gives being to the will's action together with the will, and keeps that action in being. God's cooperation here is therefore not something other than our act of will; it is our act of will itself, insofar as its production and preservation depend directly on God.

choices.why: The Schools' term for God's acting together with secondary causes; 'concurrence' keeps it recognizable as the technical term, with 'cooperation' kept for cooperatio.
